lessons.title: Computer Networks: Ring Topology & Token Passing
lessons.subject: Computer Science
lessons.description: Detailed exploration of Token Ring network architecture (IEEE 802.5), deterministic media access control, token circulation mechanics, station failure modes, MAU bypass relays, and latency calculations.

transcriptSegments.speaker: Prof. Rao
transcriptSegments.text: Good morning everyone. Today we are examining deterministic media access protocols, focusing directly on the Token Ring topology standardized under IEEE 802.5. Look up at the board diagram.

transcriptSegments.speaker: Prof. Rao
transcriptSegments.text: Notice how all workstations—labeled Station A through Station D on our visual diagram—are wired in a closed, unidirectional loop. Data frames and the control token flow in only one direction, clockwise here.

transcriptSegments.speaker: Prof. Rao
transcriptSegments.text: A special 3-byte frame called the Token continuously circles the ring. When Station A wants to transmit data to Station C, it must capture the free token, flip the busy bit from zero to one, and append its data packet.

transcriptSegments.speaker: Prof. Rao
transcriptSegments.text: Station B receives the frame, inspects the destination MAC address, sees it is meant for Station C, regenerates the signal, and forwards it along. No collision can ever occur because only the token holder transmits.

transcriptSegments.speaker: Prof. Rao
transcriptSegments.text: Now look at the textbook slide where it says: "Station C Disconnected: Entire Ring Down". Historically, a pure physical ring had a fatal single point of failure—if any cable severed, the loop broke.

transcriptSegments.speaker: Prof. Rao
transcriptSegments.text: However, please correct this limitation in your notes! Real-world deployments use a Multistation Access Unit or MAU. The physical topology is actually a star, with an electromechanical relay that instantly bypasses any powered-down or severed station.

concepts.name: Deterministic Access vs Collision
concepts.description: Unlike CSMA/CD in Ethernet where stations compete and collide, Token Ring uses a circulating authorization token ensuring maximum bounded transmission delay and zero collisions.

concepts.name: Token Circulation & Busy Bit
concepts.description: A 3-byte control frame with Starting Delimiter, Access Control byte, and Ending Delimiter. The token bit in the Access Control byte indicates whether the token is free (0) or busy carrying data (1).

concepts.name: Physical Star vs Logical Ring (MAU)
concepts.description: While logically data circulates in a ring, modern physical implementation uses a Multistation Access Unit (MAU) forming a physical star where relays automatically bypass severed nodes.

concepts.name: Single Point of Failure Vulnerability
concepts.description: A traditional pure ring topology suffers complete failure if any single link or station cable is broken, requiring active bypass or dual-counter-rotating rings (FDDI).

concepts.name: Deterministic Flow Protocol
concepts.description: System rules governing authorized transmission sequences without packet collision.

concepts.name: Single Link Vulnerability
concepts.description: Architectural risk where disruption of an individual pathway compromises system continuity.

studyArtifacts.title: Token Ring Network Architecture & Media Access
studyArtifacts.content:
## 1. Executive Summary
Token Ring (IEEE 802.5) is a deterministic local area network protocol where stations pass a 3-byte token frame in a closed unidirectional loop. Unlike Ethernet CSMA/CD, no data packet collisions can occur.

## 2. Key Components & Visual Evidence
- **Logical Topology**: Unidirectional closed ring with clockwise signal propagation (Diagram: Station A → B → C → D).
- **Workstations**: Repeaters with a 1-bit delay that inspect destination MAC addresses.
- **Token Format**:
  - Starting Delimiter (1 Byte)
  - Access Control (1 Byte, containing Priority bits, Reservation bits, and Token/Busy bit)
  - Ending Delimiter (1 Byte)

## 3. Discrepancy & Critical Correction
- **Visual Claim**: Slide warning asserts a single severed cable brings down the entire network.
- **Spoken Clarification (Prof. Rao @ 03:36)**: In practice, networks use a **Multistation Access Unit (MAU)** forming a physical star with automatic electromechanical bypass relays.

## 4. Deterministic Performance Characteristics
- Maximum bounded packet transmission delay.
- Guaranteed bandwidth allocation via priority and reservation bits.

studyArtifacts.title: Token Ring Core Revision Flashcards
studyArtifacts.content: Interactive flashcards covering Token Ring mechanics, MAU bypass, and IEEE 802.5 standard.

flashcards.question: What is the standard IEEE specification for Token Ring networks?
How many bytes comprise a free Token frame, and what are its three fields?
flashcards.answer: 3 bytes total: Starting Delimiter (1B), Access Control (1B), and Ending Delimiter (1B).

flashcards.question: How do modern Token Ring networks prevent the single-cable-cut failure mode shown on slides?
flashcards.answer: They deploy Multistation Access Units (MAUs) in a physical star topology with internal relays that automatically bypass broken or inactive stations.

flashcards.question: Why are collisions impossible in a healthy Token Ring topology?
flashcards.answer: Access is deterministic; only the station currently holding the captured token is permitted to transmit data.

studyArtifacts.title: Practice Quiz: Token Ring & Deterministic MAC
studyArtifacts.content: Multiple-choice practice questions grounded in lecture audio and slide evidence.

quiz.question: What action does a station take upon capturing a free token to transmit data?
options: Broadcasts a beacon frame to all stations
Flips the token busy bit from 0 to 1 and appends its data payload
Sends an RTS/CTS handshake packet to Station D
quiz.explanation: As explained in Audio Segment 03, the station flips the token bit in the Access Control byte from 0 (free) to 1 (busy) and appends data and destination address.

quiz.question: According to the lecture clarification, why is the slide warning ("Single Cable Cut Disables Entire Loop") misleading for practical deployments?
options: The cables used in Token Ring are indestructible optical glass
Each station contains a backup radio transceiver
MAUs wire the network as a physical star and bypass severed nodes with relays
Token Ring automatically converts to Ethernet bus mode
quiz.explanation: Prof. Rao explicitly noted that physical star wiring via MAUs uses electromechanical relays to automatically bypass disconnected stations.

quiz.question: In the lecture diagram, which station acts as the primary receiver for Station A’s transmission?
quiz.explanation: The diagram and transcript segment 03 explicitly specify Station A transmitting to Station C, with Station B acting as an intermediate repeater.
